newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pulled diplomat from Russia after car crash.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pulled diplomat from Russia after car crash.

text.p: The United States admitted Tuesday that it had hastily withdrawn a diplomat involved in a fatal car accident in Moscow in 1993 in an incident somewhat similar to a current diplomatic immunity case in Washington.

The State Department said it had pulled out the unnamed diplomat within 36 hours of the accident, in which a Russian woman was killed by the car he was driving, to avoid possible prosecution by the Russian authorities.

The department disclosed the incident as it awaited a police report on a five-vehicle collision in Washington last Friday that was started by a car driven by Georgian diplomat Gueorgui Makharadze. A 16-year-old American girl, Joviane Waltrick, died in the crash.

Spokesman Glyn Davies said the State Department could take no action until it received the report and a letter from the U.S. Attorney's office stating whether a prosecution was planned against Makharadze, 35.

If so, the department is expected to ask the Georgian government to waive Makharadze's diplomatic immunity. But U.S. officials say they do not expect Tbilisi to agree, in which case they will ask Georgia to withdraw the diplomat.

The case has caused an outcry in Washington over the whole concept of diplomatic immunity. Republican Senator Judd Gregg of New Hampshire Monday urged President Bill Clinton to withhold aid to Georgia until it waived Makharadze's immunity.
Davies said that in the Moscow case in May 1993, an American diplomat driving after midnight struck a woman pedestrian who later died in a hospital.

"We were told by the Russian government that they would prosecute this individual if the individual stayed. So we removed the individual within about 36 hours of the incident," Davies told a news briefing.

Russian authorities had believed that alcohol might have been involved, but a U.S. investigator had established that it was not, Davies said. No disciplinary action was taken against the diplomat who is still employed by the U.S. government.
Washington police are investigating whether alcohol was involved in the Makharadze case.
U.S. officials have defended diplomatic immunity as protecting American diplomats who might otherwise be the target of malicious prosecutions in authoritarian countries.

Officials were able to recall only one case of the United States waiving diplomatic immunity of an American accused of a serious offence in another country. In that case, in Bolivia in 1995, the United States itself was the aggrieved party.

The U.S. embassy in La Paz waived the immunity of David Duchow, a contractor in a U.S. government drug enforcement programme, and asked Bolivian authorities to prosecute him on charges of embezzling funds destined for the programme.
The case is still pending in Bolivia and Duchow has sued the U.S. government in a Texas court, officials said.
